title: Jeremiah 34:8–22
context: The narrator explains that King Zedekiah had made a covenant with the people of Jerusalem to proclaim liberty, so that everyone would free his Hebrew male and female servants (34:8–9). The princes and people obeyed, but afterward took the freed servants back into subjection (34:10–11). The LORD’s word through Jeremiah recalls the covenant made when he brought their fathers out of Egypt, that a Hebrew servant should go free after six years of service (34:13–14; compare Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12), and notes that their fathers did not listen. The people had turned and done right, making a covenant in the LORD’s house, but then turned back and profaned his name (34:15–16). With bitter wordplay the LORD proclaims to them “a liberty… to the sword, to the pestilence, and to the famine” (34:17). Those who broke the covenant had cut a calf in two and passed between its parts (34:18–19; compare the divided animals of Genesis 15:9–17), and they will be given to their enemies (34:20). The unit ends with the word that the king of Babylon’s army, which had gone away, will return and burn the city (34:21–22; compare 37:5, 37:11). The issue is covenant faithfulness under siege. Both traditions read it as shared ground: God holds his people to the promises they make before him, especially toward the vulnerable.

verses.text: The word came to Jeremiah from the LORD, after King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people who were at Jerusalem, to proclaim liberty to them,
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah made a covenant with the people “to proclaim liberty.” Arminian readers note the good beginning. Under siege, the king and people took a step of obedience toward the law concerning Hebrew servants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a genuine, if short-lived, act of covenant obedience. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing a real act of liberation, made by covenant, which sets up the sad reversal described in 34:11.

verses.text: that every man should let his male servant, and every man his female servant, who is a Hebrew or a Hebrewess, go free, that no one should make bondservants of them, of a Jew his brother.
verses.arminianNotes: Every Hebrew male and female servant was to go free, so that no one would enslave a fellow Jew. Arminian readers note the emphasis on brotherhood. The release rests on the bond between members of the covenant people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the law protected fellow Israelites from permanent servitude (compare Deuteronomy 15:12). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse in its covenant setting, and neither turns it into a modern political program.

verses.text: All the princes and all the people obeyed who had entered into the covenant, that everyone should let his male servant and everyone his female servant go free, that no one should make bondservants of them any more. They obeyed and let them go,
verses.arminianNotes: The princes and people obeyed and let their servants go. Arminian readers note that the obedience was real. The people did what was right, which makes their later reversal all the more serious.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the genuine obedience recorded here. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the people knew what was right and did it for a time, setting up the reversal that follows.

verses.text: but afterwards they turned, and caused the servants and the handmaids whom they had let go free to return, and brought them into subjection for servants and for handmaids.
verses.arminianNotes: The text says “afterwards they turned,” and brought the freed servants back into subjection. Arminian readers note the tragedy of obedience abandoned. The people chose to reverse what they had done before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the fickleness of a heart that obeys under pressure and turns back afterward. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober example of broken faithfulness, and both see its seriousness in the harm done to the vulnerable.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah.” Arminian readers note that the LORD responds to the people’s reversal. Their actions are seen and answered, showing that covenant promises made before God matter to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s word responding to covenant breaking. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing the LORD’s judgment on the broken covenant, which the following verses explain.

verses.text: “The LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I made a covenant with your fathers in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage, saying:
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD recalls the covenant made when he brought their fathers “out of the house of bondage.” Arminian readers note the fitting reminder: a people freed from slavery should not keep their brothers in bondage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the exodus as the ground of the law of release. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as rooting the command in God’s own act of redemption, which calls his people to show the same mercy to others.

verses.text: At the end of seven years, every man of you shall release his brother who is a Hebrew, who has been sold to you, and has served you six years. You shall let him go free from you. But your fathers didn’t listen to me, and didn’t incline their ear.
verses.arminianNotes: At the end of seven years, a Hebrew servant who served six years was to go free. Arminian readers note the law behind the covenant (compare Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12), and that their fathers did not listen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the law of release and the long history of neglecting it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as citing the covenant command, and neither turns this unit into a wider debate about the law beyond what the text says.

verses.text: You had now turned, and had done that which is right in my eyes, in every man proclaiming liberty to his neighbor. You had made a covenant before me in the house which is called by my name;
verses.arminianNotes: “You had now turned, and had done that which is right in my eyes.” Arminian readers note the LORD’s approval of their repentance. Their turning was real and pleasing to him, made by covenant in his house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s approval of genuine obedience. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as recognizing a right act, and both see the covenant made “in the house which is called by my name” as raising the seriousness of breaking it.

verses.text: but you turned and profaned my name, and every man caused his servant and every man his handmaid, whom you had let go free at their pleasure, to return. You brought them into subjection, to be to you for servants and for handmaids.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “but you turned and profaned my name.” Arminian readers note that breaking the covenant dishonors God himself. Taking back the freed servants was not only harm to them but contempt for the promise made before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the profaning of God’s name in breaking a sworn covenant. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as joining harm to neighbor and dishonor to God, and both see the vulnerability of the servants as central to the offense.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD says: “You have not listened to me, to proclaim liberty, every man to his brother, and every man to his neighbor. Behold, I proclaim to you a liberty,” says the LORD, “to the sword, to the pestilence, and to the famine. I will make you be tossed back and forth among all the kingdoms of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I proclaim to you a liberty… to the sword, to the pestilence, and to the famine.” Arminian readers note the bitter wordplay. The people refused liberty to others, so they will receive a terrible “liberty” in judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment fitted to the offense. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as a measure-for-measure judgment, and both see in it the seriousness with which God treats the denial of freedom to the vulnerable.

verses.text: I will give the men who have transgressed my covenant, who have not performed the words of the covenant which they made before me when they cut the calf in two and passed between its parts:
verses.arminianNotes: They “cut the calf in two and passed between its parts.” Arminian readers note the solemn covenant ritual, which seems to invoke the fate of the animal on those who break it (compare Genesis 15:9–17). The text reports it soberly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a covenant sealed with a self-curse, and note the comparison with Genesis 15. Shared ground: both traditions report the ritual soberly and read the verse as showing the gravity of the promise the people broke.

verses.text: the princes of Judah, the princes of Jerusalem, the eunuchs, the priests, and all the people of the land, who passed between the parts of the calf.
verses.arminianNotes: Princes, eunuchs, priests, and all the people passed between the parts of the calf. Arminian readers note that every level of society shared in the covenant and so shares in the guilt of breaking it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the whole community bound by the oath. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as naming those accountable for the broken covenant, and neither expands on the ritual beyond what the text reports.

verses.text: I will even give them into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their life. Their dead bodies will be food for the birds of the sky and for the animals of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: They will be given to their enemies, and their bodies will be food for birds and animals. Arminian readers note the covenant curse coming upon those who broke the covenant. The text is reported soberly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the self-curse of the covenant ritual fulfilled. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with pastoral sobriety, neither softening nor dwelling on its details, and see it as the consequence of covenant unfaithfulness.

verses.text: “I will give Zedekiah king of Judah and his princes into the hands of their enemies, into the hands of those who seek their life and into the hands of the king of Babylon’s army, who has gone away from you.
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah and his princes will be given to the king of Babylon’s army, “who has gone away from you.” Arminian readers note the temporary relief of the siege (compare 37:5, 37:11). The people may have thought the danger had passed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the withdrawal of the army as no real deliverance. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse alongside 37:5 and 37:11, and both see the reversal of the slave release as happening in a moment of false relief.

verses.text: Behold, I will command,” says the LORD, “and cause them to return to this city. They will fight against it, take it, and burn it with fire. I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant.”
verses.arminianNotes: “I will command… and cause them to return to this city.” Arminian readers note that the LORD announces the return of the army. The relief will end, and the city will be taken and burned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s sovereign command over the movements of the armies. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sure word of judgment on the city, and the question of how God directs the nations is treated at Judges 9:23.
